passages.happening:
In the third year of Hoshea of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz becomes king of Judah at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done’ (verse 3).

He removes the high places, shatters the sacred pillars and cuts down the Asherah poles. ‘He also demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it’ (verse 4). ‘Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him’ (verse 5). The LORD is with him, and he prospers. He rebels against the king of Assyria and defeats the Philistines as far as Gaza (verses 7-8).

The narrator tells again how Shalmaneser besieged Samaria in Hezekiah's fourth year and took it in his sixth (verses 9-11). ‘This happened because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The book has just told of the north's end, and Judah now faces the same empire. Ahaz met the Assyrian threat by becoming Assyria's servant. His son does the opposite, and the narrator praises him more highly than any king since David. Verses 9 to 12 repeat the fall of Samaria on purpose, to set Hezekiah's story in its shadow. Chapters 18 to 20 are found again, with small differences, in Isaiah 36 to 39.

Hezekiah's dates are a famous puzzle. Verse 1 places his accession around 727 BC, but verse 13 puts Sennacherib's invasion, securely dated to 701 BC, in his fourteenth year, which would place it around 715 BC. Scholars solve it in different ways, most often by proposing a time when he shared the throne with Ahaz, or by preferring one of the two dates. The site's guide to the kings gives 716 or 715 to 687 or 686 BC.

The bronze snake was the one Moses made in the wilderness, which healed those who looked at it. Over the centuries it had become an object of worship. Its name, Nehushtan, sounds like the Hebrew words for bronze and snake, and some take it as Hezekiah's dismissive label: it is only a piece of bronze. A good gift of God becomes an idol when it is worshiped instead of the God who gave it.

The key word of chapters 18 and 19 is trust, batach. It describes Hezekiah in verse 5, and the enemy's whole strategy is to break it.
passages.later: In the wilderness, ‘If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live’ (Numbers 21:9). Jesus said, ‘Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up’ (John 3:14).
passages.asks: Hezekiah broke up a bronze snake that had once been a real means of God's healing. Ask what good things in your life or your church are receiving the trust that belongs to God. And ask what it would cost you to break them.

passages.t: Tribute stripped from the temple doors
passages.happening:
‘In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah’ (verse 13). Hezekiah sends word to him at Lachish: “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me” (verse 14). The king of Assyria demands three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold (verse 14).

Hezekiah gives him all the silver in the house of the LORD and the palace treasuries (verse 15). He strips the gold with which he had plated the doors and doorposts of the temple and gives it to the king of Assyria (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC. When he came to the throne, several western vassals, Hezekiah among them, stopped paying tribute, and in 701 BC he marched west. His own annals, preserved on clay prisms, describe the campaign. He claims to have taken forty-six of Hezekiah's fortified cities and to have shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and he lists tribute that included thirty talents of gold, the same figure as verse 14; his figure for silver is higher. The annals do not claim that Jerusalem was taken.

Lachish was Judah's second city. Sennacherib had its siege carved in stone reliefs for his palace at Nineveh, and excavations at Lachish have uncovered the Assyrian siege ramp and a destruction layer from this campaign.
passages.later: Isaiah begins the same story with the same words: ‘In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah’ (Isaiah 36:1).
passages.hard:
Why does Hezekiah, who trusted the LORD, pay tribute and strip the temple doors?

These verses are striking right after the praise of verses 5 to 7. Hezekiah admits he has done wrong, pays an enormous sum, and strips even the gold he had put on the temple doors. Some readers see a lapse of faith, much like Ahaz's payment to Tiglath-pileser, and they note that it did not work: the Assyrians came to Jerusalem anyway. Others read it as a responsible king's attempt to spare his people when his land was already overrun, not a denial of trust in the LORD.

The narrator does not comment, which leaves both readings open. What the story does show is that paying off the empire did not buy safety. The rescue of Jerusalem in the next chapter comes not from Hezekiah's payment but from his prayer.
passages.asks: Hezekiah tried to buy peace and found the empire wanted more. Ask where you have tried to buy safety with what belonged to God. And ask what you do when the price you paid does not bring the peace you hoped for.

passages.happening:
The king of Assyria sends the Tartan, the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to Jerusalem. They stand by the aqueduct of the upper pool, and three of Hezekiah's officials go out to them (verses 17-18). The Rabshakeh says, ‘What is the basis of this confidence of yours?’ (verse 19). Strategy and strength are empty words. Egypt is ‘that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’ (verse 21). And the LORD, he says, is the god whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed (verse 22). He offers two thousand horses, if Judah can find riders for them (verse 23). He even claims that the LORD sent him (verse 25).

The officials ask him to speak in Aramaic, not in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall (verse 26). Instead he calls out loudly in Hebrew to the people: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand” (verse 29). Make peace and come out, he says, and each of them will eat from his own vine and fig tree until he takes them to a land like their own (verses 31-32). ‘Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?’ (verse 33). ‘How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?’ (verse 35).

‘But the people remained silent and did not answer a word’ (verse 36), for Hezekiah had told them not to answer. The officials come to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and tell him what was said (verses 36-37).
passages.hearers:
The three Assyrian officials carry titles, not names. The Tartan was the army's commander in chief, the Rabsaris a senior court official, and the Rabshakeh, literally chief cupbearer, a high officer who acts here as spokesman. Speaking to a besieged city's people over the heads of its leaders was a known tactic of psychological war. Aramaic was the language of diplomacy in the Assyrian empire, understood by officials but not by ordinary Judeans, which is why the officials ask for it and why he refuses.

His speech is shrewd. He knows about Judah's hope in Egypt and mocks it. He knows that Hezekiah has closed the high places, and he twists the reform into an offense against the LORD. His claim that the LORD sent him may reflect knowledge of prophets like Isaiah, who had called Assyria the rod of God's anger. Every man under his own vine and fig tree was Israel's own picture of peace, and he offers it as the reward for surrender, followed by deportation.

The speech closes off every hope in turn: not strategy, not Egypt, not the LORD, not Hezekiah, not any god of any nation. The word deliver, natsal, runs through it again and again. Its last question puts the LORD on the level of the gods of Hamath and Arpad, and the next chapter answers it. The chapter ends in silence.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7). Micah promised the peace the Rabshakeh counterfeited: ‘each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree, with no one to frighten him’ (Micah 4:4).
passages.asks: The Rabshakeh's speech worked by closing off every hope one by one. Ask how you answer the voices, inside or outside you, that say your trust in God is foolish. And ask when silence, like the people's on the wall, is the wisest answer to mockery.
